title: Dongshan's Companion
speaker: Eko Jeff Kelley
summary: The talk's main teaching emphasizes the importance of cultivating a "companion" within oneself, rather than trying to grasp external concepts or ideas. This companion is not something that can be constructed or grasped, but rather an energy of loyalty and openness that allows us to show up in each moment with sincerity and humility. By developing this inner companion, we can invite our true nature into being and meet it with compassion and kindness, allowing us to embody the qualities of mindfulness, determination, and openness in our daily lives.

sentences.text: Good morning, everyone.
Nice to see you all.
What a solid group we are, right?
It's a pleasure to be here with both sanghas and all the guests.
Yesterday Tim was actually able to give us some encouraging words about the state of the world amongst the discouragement, and helped us ground our practice in what's going on right now in the world.

Then he told the story about Nyogen Senzaki, an early Zen pioneer in America, and how he lived this long life of, well, continuous dedication and effort, but there weren't a lot of fruits that he saw.
I think that's inspiring, to make effort regardless of what fruits seem to be appearing, because we really have no idea what the effects of our practice are.
His memorial service was, as we understand it, the first Zen sesshin in America.
But he didn't know about it, right?
He was already dead.
And his practice continued on in a strong way.
Who knows what he thought while he was alive?
I'm told that Katagiri Roshi considered his work to be a failure in America, at least at some times.
And here we are today, here I am today, and his dharma has spread widely.
So if you find yourself thinking that you are powerless in the face of all the tragic events, don't believe it.
Don't buy into that story.
You don't know the effect of one act of kindness.
We never lose the power to influence the world for the better.
So don't believe in a story about your own powerlessness.
Today I want to share another story about effort.

This story seems to me good for when we're deeper in sesshin, when we've, for the moment, set the events of the world aside and prepare to celebrate Buddha's enlightenment, to celebrate our own original nature, to go deeply into that matter.
So my story today is about Dongshan.
If we can point to anyone as the founder of the Soto tradition, I think it has to be Dongshan.
He is the Dung in the [unclear: "Kao Dung"] school, as it's called in Chinese, and he is To or Tozan in Japanese.
So he is the To in our Soto lineage.
There are many stories about Dongshan.
Before he began to study with the master who would eventually give him transmission, he went to Nanquan's assembly.
Nanquan was a disciple of the great Matsu, who is known for his powerful bearing, his strong presentation of the Dharma and his many students.
Dongshan was young and had just arrived in this group and was checking things out.
He happened to be there on the anniversary of Matsu's death, and the congregation was working to prepare a feast in honor of Matsu, honoring the late teacher as was customary.
Nanquan went before the assembly and said, "Tomorrow we will have Matsu's feast.
Will Matsu come or not?"
We're having a ceremony for Matsu.
Will he come?
He is dead.
Will he come?
Nobody had much to say in the assembly except this rash young man in the back row, Dongshan, and he said, "If he has a companion, he'll come."
Will Matsu come?
If he has a companion, he will come.
This story has always intrigued me.
Also unsettled me.
Early on I thought it was calling me to do something that I didn't think I could do.
But I've come to look at it a little differently now.
It goes on a little bit.
Nanquan replies, "Whoa," more laughs.
He says, "Although this is a young man, he is suitable for polishing."
And Dongshan replied, at least in one version, "Please don't try to make a free servant into a slave."
So there's a little interesting interplay.
But today we're going to stay with the preparing of a ceremony for Matsu.
Will he come?
If he has a companion, he will come.
So there's a certain kind of energy and a certain kind of effort that's being pointed to.
But what is it exactly?
I would like to emphasize it's not just about being the brash young Zen student in the back row, ready to step forward and take on the master.
Although if there are such beings present, that would be fine too.
But I'm not; somebody else is in that seat.
It's the idea of a companion, of this personage, this energy that we make into a personage, setting the feast, issuing the invitation, and manifesting as a companion.
This idea of companion in our tradition interests me a lot.
I think because we are a non-theistic tradition, we don't have anybody to talk to really or ask questions of.
So underneath that non-theistic overlay, we have created a number of personages: our bodhisattvas, [unclear: "the Loki, Tesvara"] and Manjusri, and many ancestors and many stories.
I think this speaks to a basic characteristic of our psyches, that we relate to our experience in this way.
We create these personages in order to convey a teaching, in order to convey an experience, in order to inspire.
A myth, you might call it, in a good sense of the word.
Thich Nhat Hanh has another version of the companion.
He speaks of mindfulness as a gentle companion.
Quite a different energy, I think.
Speaking of mindfulness, he says:
*This awareness is a companion for the anger.
Our mindful observation is not to suppress or drive out our anger, but just to look after it.
This is a very important principle in meditation practice.
Mindful observation is like a lamp that gives light.
It is not a judge.
It throws light on our anger, sponsors it, looks after it in an affectionate and caring way, like an older sister looking after and comforting her younger sibling.*
When I was younger, I would be somewhat dismissive of that, perhaps, as maybe too soft.
But the more I practice, the more wise and deep that open-hearted taking care of energy is for me.
And it's really not different from the bold meeting that Dongshan embodies.
It feels different sometimes.
I have this curious story and curious idea of inviting.
In this case, the ceremony is inviting Matsu to come.
What are we inviting?
And how are we going to show up to be a companion?
It raises a lot of interesting questions, I think.
This last day of sesshin, what have you been inviting?
Who or what have you been inviting?
And who or what has been showing up to meet it?
We know that sesshin, in general, is kind of an invitation to our demons, to Mara.
When Buddha, before he was enlightened, the story goes, sat up under the Bodhi tree and resolved to awaken, and wouldn't get up until he saw the truth, Mara's antennas went up immediately.
"Okay, we'll see about that."

And he came and assailed Shakyamuni Buddha, first with desire, then with fear, and finally with the sense of unworthiness, until Shakyamuni Buddha touched the earth and tapped into the strength, the energy of all beings.
And Mara was, you could say, vanquished, or you could just say he settled down.
So I think when we sit down on our cushion for sesshin, whether we intend it or not, we kind of issue an invitation to our demons.
We say, "Okay, I'm here.
I don't necessarily want to see you," but we learn that they come, right?
As we resolve to awaken, as we resolve to sit upright and still, they come.
So how do we meet them?
How do we meet that judgmental mind, that sense of unworthiness?
First of all, it helps to recognize it as a familiar.
You can use the word demon or you can use some other word, but it's a familiar counterpart that has come forth and needs to be met with a different kind of energy in order to further open to life.
So when these thoughts come in, it can be like a little alarm: "Oh, there it is again."
Can I meet it with this energy that Thich Nhat Hanh described, an affectionate and caring way, or at least a resolute one?
The two really come together.
Sometimes these demons are so strong that we just need strong resolve in order to be present with this discomfort.
A little bit of that warrior energy is necessary to stay on our seat.
It's not that we're fighting anything, but we need some strong resolve in order to stay on our seat.
And we also need that soft heart that Thich Nhat Hanh points to.
How have you been meeting these things?
Have you been noticing unkindness in your own thought patterns and meeting it not with more unkindness, but with kindness, with acceptance and tolerance and encouragement?
So these two aspects of energy: this invitation, if you will, and the showing up as a companion.
I have to acknowledge there are lots of pitfalls in this presentation of teaching.
We don't want to be conjuring up specific personages and having a conversation with them.
It's not really what we're talking about, although a little bit of that could be okay.
What is the effort that is involved in inviting?
Inviting Matsu, inviting...
Perhaps we would invite Ling Zhao.
Ling Zhao is the daughter of Laman Pong and Lei Wuman Pong.
You may know this story.
Laman Pong was sitting in a [unclear: "statch"] cottage one day praying the sutras.
"Difficult, difficult, difficult," he suddenly exclaimed.
"Like trying to store [unclear: "ten bushes of sesame seed"] in the top of a tree."
Or perhaps like [unclear: "oriochi"], right?
"Difficult, difficult, difficult."
His wife, Lei Wuman Pong, we're calling her: "Easy, easy, easy," his wife answered.
"It's like touching your feet to the floor when you get out of bed."
If we are open to seeing it.
The daughter, Ling Zhao, usually has the last word, a niece.
"Neither difficult nor easy," she said.
"It's like the teachings of the ancestors shining on the hundred grass tips."

There's a little bit of a mystery there, but there's also some freshness, some openness, some invitation to the ancestors, and the teachings appear on the tips of the hundred grasses, that is, everywhere we look.
So perhaps we'll invite Ling Zhao to come.
Perhaps you want to invite Ling Zhao rather than Matsu or Shakyamuni.
There are lots of good candidates, but really we're talking about inviting true nature.
What is that?
What would that be like?
Inviting.
How could we do that without falling into the weeds, without grasping and construction and all such things that we have learned cause suffering?
So that invitation or openness is a subtle thing.
I suggest that for all of us, it's a koan.
What is it?
How do I open?
How do I make it possible?
An invitation is in part a sense of the possibilities or, put another way, a letting go of the impossibilities.
You might say, "Well, I don't know this person, this Ling Zhao, this Matsu, this true nature.
I really don't know what they're like."
But I would suggest that they may be somewhat unfamiliar in your present life, but they're not unknown.
Maybe they're just unremembered, unacknowledged, unhonored.
So part of this energy of invitation, I think, is honoring the subtle knowings that may just be at the periphery of our awareness, or they may be front and center for a moment.
The subtle knowings that we might tend to dismiss: "Oh, that's nothing.
How can that be anything?
Because it's gone."
These glimpses and these calls.
What called you to come here to sesshin this weekend or today?
Something deep in your heart, some glimmer of true nature, some idea of the possibility of meeting our life in a different way.
Not even an idea, but an unremembered certainty.
We might call this faith.
Some traditions, I think, we do have that teaching in our tradition: great faith, great doubt, great determination.
Faith that you are Buddha, that your true nature is luminous and open and engaged.
So we do have little glimpses, little tastes, little insights, little knowings of this sort.
Otherwise, why would we be here?
It would be crazy, right?
So, remembering to come back to that sense of possibility, that sense of openness, that sense of wonder, that sense of faith.
And yet we're so loyal to our bad habits, aren't we?
Our mental patterns.
We just return to them like, "Oh yeah, I'm back.
Judgment, yeah, feels right at home.
Unworthiness, criticism, anger, yeah.
I think I'll indulge in that for a while."
We're really loyal to that part of ourselves.
We just zoom right back.
So part of this energy of invitation is developing a little loyalty to this other part of ourselves, this other, more subtle, more unremembered, deeper calling.
We can call it Matsu, we can call it Ling Zhao, we can call it original face.
What is it like to sit here and be open to that?
It's a little different than being open to anything.
And maybe some people would say that was a problem, but to be open without solidifying, without concretizing, without telling ourselves a story about it.
Just be open to that sense that is brought with these subtle knowings, these glimpses, these deep callings.
Every one of us has this true nature, participates in this true nature, has it welling up inside of them.
So we zazen, you might say, is a ceremony in honor of true nature.
Will it come?
If it has a companion, it will come.
So we have this energy of showing up as a companion, mainly just showing up.
When Matsu comes, or when Mara comes, our demons, we're kind of familiar with that; we still have to show up.
And this other, more subtle thing that we might even be grasping after, although grasping after is not the invitation that we're talking about.
The invitation is, well, it's like having a campfire in the dark woods.
Or it's like, and I'm thinking the animals draw near.
Or it's like sitting quietly in the woods and allowing the woods to come alive as we sit quietly.
It's that kind of invitation.
Alive with birds and wind and mushrooms and everything else.
Foxes.
So the energy to show up, as I said before, sometimes requires some vigilance.
It's like, "Okay, I see that mind, that critical mind again.
I'm going to do something.
I see the unkindness.
I'm going to not perpetuate it with more unkindness.
I'm going to turn and bring kindness to that."
Sometimes that needs to be a strong energy, and some vigilance pays off.
How long are we going to indulge in our unwholesome thought patterns that keep us from loving this world, from meeting this life directly?
So we show up with a degree of strength and also a degree of softness.
And of course, from another perspective, this invitation and this showing up are one and the same.
But for me, looking at them as split brings forth some subtlety to both sides, different aspects of that energy.
Our tradition also teaches us that call and response arise together.
So this is not to muddy the waters here, but the companion and Matsu arrive together.
The companion and Lingzhao arrive together.
But we don't really have to worry about that.
We do our part, and the universe responds.
It's not because we're good or we get it exactly right, or we finally do zazen, or zazen is finally so good that something wonderful happens.
That's not really what we're talking about.
We're talking about that open, honoring invitation and that sincere diligence showing up.
Today and this weekend and the rest of the day and tonight and tomorrow morning, we are having a celebration for Shakyamuni Buddha, right?
Honoring the enlightenment of the Buddha.
Honoring the enlightenment of all beings.
So we have to ask, will he show up?
Will true nature show up?
If there is a companion, can we lay the feast?
Try not to get biblical here, but can we put out the feast?
Can we issue the invitation?
Can we sit upright and just entertain that mind of limitless possibility, and then show up in each moment?
Show up with determination, show up with soft, loving heart.
And who knows what will happen?
Who knows what it looks like?
Who knows what it feels like?
We don't need to know.
That's another important ingredient of both sides of our effort: the not knowing.
Will true nature show up if it has a companion?
